IN THE GARDEN OF
GOOD AND EVIL
RICK JAMES

Writing on the problem of evil is like that. The reader
holds in tension two separate categories for critique:
do you have any real wisdom on the subject, and
what do you know about pain anyway? Well if you
want to know, have I had anyone beat on my pelvis
with a baseball bat for 26 hours, no, I haven’t. But I’ve
experienced enough pain to know the wisdom of this
saying: “pain is pain.” Which means pain is always
relative to your life. It might be painful for Bill Gates
to stay in Super 8 Hotel, who knows, and that’s the
point, we don’t have to know, or more specifically
we don’t have to judge—“pain is pain” and we’ve all
experienced it—no one gets out of life alive.
Who put the fun in the funhouse?
You did, baby - you did
Who put your dad in the halfhouse?
You did, baby - you did, baby
Who dug the hole in the outhouse?

Who put Whitey in the White House?

Keep a Lid on Things, Crash Test Dummies
Well, flowing from my first edict of wisdom that
“pain is pain,” I shall now utter a second oracle: the
problem of evil can’t be answered. It is a mystery,
and not a problem. We shed light on mysteries: we
solve problems. I do believe we can shed light on the
mystery of evil, but even as we do, we’ll notice that as
the circle of light grows larger in its circumference
so does the surrounding darkness, meaning answers
will generate more questions and at some point we
will just need to cease: you from reading, and me from
writing.
I was listening to a conversation between mothers
concerning childbirth. One woman claimed, “It was
like having someone beat on my spinal cord with a
baseball bat…for 26 hours.” A clear hierarchy began
to emerge: those who had suffered, and those who
So I’ve redefined our search. We are not looking
for an answer, but insight or clues that allow us to
apprehend, in some way, why God would allow evil. I
just realized I have not mentioned God hitherto, but of

course without God there is no problem: the world is
what it is, and evil is simply a word we use to describe
what “it is” we don’t like. The mystery we are trying
to solve is why a good and loving God would allow the
world to be “as it is.”
reformer like Martin Luther King appealing to when
he indicts society for acting immorally. Clearly, it
must be a standard above or outside the society. Don’t
we sense that helping a child is right and abusing one
is wrong? Our minds are a virtual filing cabinet for the
folders of what is good and what is evil.
I’ve decided that we are going to approach this
by way of the backdoor. That is, we’ll begin by
presupposing that the correct verdict to the mystery
is that the existence of a good and loving God is
truly incompatible with evil; they are divorced on
grounds of irreconcilable differences. What sorts
of existential and philosophical problems have we
created for ourselves by solving the problem through
the elimination of God?
I have raised a zillion issues, philosophically, some
are legitimate points and others are not. I’ll let you
figure out which is which. All in all, using good
common horse sense—which I don’t believe evolved
from a horse—I’m not happy with the problems that
eliminating God leaves me with. It’s like working on a
jigsaw puzzle and jamming two closely related pieces
together, and while those pieces couldn’t fit more
snug, the whole rest of the puzzle doesn’t fit. And so
you reason, perhaps, these pieces don’t fit together,
after all.
IF GOD ISN’T THERE
Well let’s see, if God isn’t there, we are forced to agree
with the insane notion that creativity, art, speech,
love, morality, justice, compassion and courage
evolved by happenstance. Hmm, what are the odds;
perhaps tomorrow I’ll find an iMac sprouting out of
my neck, leaving my PC head to swing in the trees of
evolutionary obsolescence. While possible, the belief
in such ingenious happenstance might take more faith
then I’ve got.
So I’m going to assume that God is there and that
evil is there and that somehow we can make the two
jigsaw pieces fit without ripping the cardboard all to
hell. Perhaps a stroke of genius or ignorance on my
part—you can be the judge of that—but it has always
seemed to me that the Scriptures (Judeo/Christian-
Old testament/New Testament) provide an insightful
perspective on the problem of evil, as opposed to other
religious books where evil came to us on the back of a
sea turtle or something to that effect.
And then there is the spiritual component of man.
Wherever you go in the world people are innately
religious. Atheism must be learned, while theism
is reflexive, as is a belief in an afterlife. But no one
has ever proved there’s an afterlife. What would you
suggest: someone die and then come back and tell us
what it was like? It’s called a Near Death Experience
and they happen all the time. There is considerable
uniformity to the experiences, and people do in
fact continue to exist though their vital signs have
flat-lined. I’m not sure what more evidence could be
provided here.
THE GOOD BOOK
The Bible does not hide the reality of human suffering
or evil, actually highlighting some of the grocer
varieties from our human history: rape, incest, human
sacrifice, torture, it’s all in there, and described in
a manner worthy of an NC-17 rating. The story of
Genesis, and Adam and Eve in particular, was meant
to communicate some fundamental truths about the
human condition: why it is, as it is, and not as it should
or could have been.
And then there are all the existential issues that
race through our curvy grey roads of cerebrum:
assumptions that life should have purpose, that people
should be loved, that we were made for something
better, that rights are inalienable. From wherest come
thy existential hard drive?
And what of the moral side of man? Don’t we sense
that torturing children is always wrong and not just
a cultural belief—well sure, if you live in Greenland I
guess torturing kids is alright. If our morality is simply
derived from our society who or what is a moral
The story encapsulates these general principles: Man
was a special creation endowed with the thumbprint
of a Creator, which was manifest among other ways
in our free will; God created something good, man
and woman, and something equally good, free will.
By its nature, free will makes for two unimaginable
possibilities: a person can freely choose to love you, as
opposed to being programmed to do so, and they could
choose to reject, even hate, even murder you.
(What comprises God’s knowledge is difficult to say,

but I believe He not only knows what will happen in
the future, but He knows all possible futures: possible
worlds he could have created including worlds where
free will did not exist. I therefore assume that out of
all possible worlds, a world containing freewill was
more desirable. And, out of all of possible worlds
where man was given freewill, this is the best possible
world: the sum total of all contingencies yielding the
greatest good however God would define “greatest
good.”)
Returning to the Garden (and if it’s any reflection
of the downward spiral of evil, I believe that
geographically theologians place the actual location of
the Garden somewhere near Falluja, Iraq), mankind
sinned and evil entered in to the Creation. Genesis
clearly states that evil was not a part of God’s original
design, but a consequence of human sin (the perverse
use of free-will). With that choice of rebellion, the
relationship between man and God was severed, and
like links in a chain it ruptured every relationship
contingent to it: man with man (wars, murder), man
with woman (divorce, broken families), man with
nature (alienation), man with himself (guilt, shame,
fear). The negative experience of these severed
relationships is what we refer to as suffering. Like a
broken DNA sequence it has produced all manner of
deformity and suffering.
As I think we’ve all noticed, the world that we live
in—the world that God actualized—might not be
optimal for happiness, but it may be optimal for
“soul-making:” the creation of great souls. I’m not
sure, for instance, where courage, compassion, mercy,
or justice might be created except in the crucible
of a bent world. These are latent human capacities
that can either be developed or not, and as we make
choices with our will, they become actual virtues. And
until we do act on them they are nothing more then
hypothetical capacities, sort of like the wings on a
turkey.
A second possible reason for allowing our current
world to have lapsed into a Mr. Smith infected Matrix
is ironically found in the final chapter of Genesis.
After witnessing the outbreak and epidemic of the
virus of human evil in chapters 1 to 49, Genesis,
chapter 50, hands us this analysis.
You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good
to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of
many lives. (Genesis 50:20)
The physics of evil seems to corroborate the biblical
sequence of events, as there is no original evil. Try as
we might, evil is always a parasite of good. You cannot
have bulimia without something good to pervert,
like eating. You cannot have destruction without
something of value to destroy. Evil is always a bent
good. In other words good must have been prior to
evil.
God, the author of creative activity, demonstrates that
the ultimate act of creation is not making something
from nothing, but making gold out of manure.
The ability to bring good out of evil is roughly the
definition of redemption. And it would seem that as
courage can only be seen in a broken world, so too
redemption. The creative activity of redemption,
the experience of being redeemed, and the virtue of
being a redeemer, are a part of why I believe God has
allowed evil. As I write this, the Super Bowl has just
ended and the coach is fighting back tears as he holds
up his humongous trophy. The victory, the battle, the
struggle, the overcoming, the joy, the relief, the peace:
perhaps God feels this makes for a better story and
existence then the living coma of nirvana—I do.
Something of the physics of our own experience
corroborates it as well: the greatest portion of evil and
suffering in the world is the result of human choices:
As of today I count 26 wars going on in the world, and
on a personal level I have envied, lied, hated, lusted
and spent $13.50 on lunch and Starbucks that could
have saved a child from starving, and that’s just since
9:00 o’clock this morning.
WHAT COULD POSSIBLEY BE WORTH IT?
If, as I have suggested, God knew the outcome of
giving us freewill, he must have seen a greater good in
allowing it, but what? Again, the Scriptures, though
far from exhaustive, provide clues.
C.S. Lewis once said that “God whispers to us in our
pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our
pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world.” The
scriptures allude that another reason God has allowed
this mosh-pit of a world is that we might “cry out” and
“return” to God. Happy and content people don’t see
their need for God, desperate people do. Trauma and
calamity shake the very foundations of our life and
force us to reexamine ourselves: our beliefs, lifestyles,
and choices.
And while we’re discussing this ideal world for soul

making it might be instructive to make an observation
about the physical laws of such a world. It would
need to operate on strict cause and effect. Think for
instance, if God were to intervene every time someone
shot a gun, turning the bullets into marshmallows
(yum). It is only in consequences and the
predictability of consequences that we are able to act
as true moral agents. I mean if God’s is always going to
keep my car from crashing, why even look where I’m
driving. A soul-making world is one of strict cause and
effect, and therefore, by design, one in which divine
intervention wars against its very purpose.
Rick James has served on staff with Campus Crusade
for Christ for over 20 years. He is currently the
publisher of CruPress.
A WORD TO THE LEFT BRAIN
While necessary, that was admittedly academic and
heartless, and yet the problem of evil is emotional as
well as intellectual. It’s not simply “why do people
suffer?’ but “Why did my mother suffer?” As a
Christian, the following passage, to me, is one of the
most powerful in the New Testament:
As he approached the town gate, a dead person was
being carried out—the only son of his mother, and she
was a widow. And a large crowd from the town was
with her. When the Lord saw her, his heart went out to
her and he said, “Don’t cry.” (Luke 7:12,13)
I find it of enormous comfort to read that Jesus’
“heart went out to her.” Intellectually it helps me to
know that God has reasons for my suffering, but I am
comforted that God is pained by my pain: that he is
not distant, uncaring, or unmoved by my suffering.
The scriptures are saturated with such expressions
of God’s compassion, the Mosaic Law going as far as
to legislate against animal suffering. I do not know
what pain you’ve experienced or what event or events
would lead you to read this article, but the message of
the Scriptures is that God deeply cares and is moved
by your suffering.
